A finite group is a list of elements. A Lie group is a smooth family of them, like the rotations, labeled by continuous parameters such as angles. You can’t write down a multiplication table for a continuum of elements, so we need a different way to get our hands on the group.

The idea of this memo is that almost everything about a Lie group can already be seen in the elements that are infinitesimally close to the identity. Those are described by a finite set of matrices, the generators. And the way the group multiplies is encoded in a finite set of numbers, the structure constants. We’ll see where the structure constants come from, why they’re all you need, and what they tell us about the group and its representations.

1Generators

Consider a continuous family of linear transformations D(α),D(\alpha)\text{,}D(α), labeled smoothly by real parameters α=(α1,α2,… ),\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)\text{,}α=(α1​,α2​,…), with D(0)=1,D(0)=1\text{,}D(0)=1, the identity transformation. Near the identity we can Taylor-expand:

D(δα)=1+i δαaXa+O(δα2),Xa≡−i∂D(α)∂αa∣α=0.D(\delta\alpha) = 1 + i\,\delta\alpha_a X_a + \order(\delta\alpha^2), \qquad X_a \equiv -i\left.\frac{\partial D(\alpha)}{\partial \alpha_a}\right|_{\alpha=0}.D(δα)=1+iδαa​Xa​+O(δα2),Xa​≡−i∂αa​∂D(α)​​α=0​.
(1)

Repeated indices are summed, here and throughout. The operators XaX_aXa​ are the generators of the group: they describe what an infinitesimal transformation looks like. The factor of iii is a convention, chosen so that the generators of unitary transformations come out Hermitian (Section 5). We take the XaX_aXa​ to be linearly independent, since otherwise some of the parameters would be redundant, and we let NNN be their number.

2The exponential parametrization

Knowing DDD only for tiny δα\delta\alphaδα isn’t much use on its own. The standard trick for turning infinitesimal information into a finite transformation is to apply an infinitesimal step many times in a row, making each step smaller as you add more of them. That’s exactly how exe^xex comes out of compound interest. So we define a new way of labeling group elements, the exponential parametrization:

D(α)≡lim⁡n→∞(1+iαaXan) ⁣n=eiαaXa.D(\alpha) \equiv \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{i\alpha_aX_a}{n}\right)^{\!n} = e^{i\alpha_aX_a}.D(α)≡n→∞lim​(1+niαa​Xa​​)n=eiαa​Xa​.
(2)

This is a choice of how the parameters label the group elements, not a consequence of the original labeling. From now on, D(α)D(\alpha)D(α) means eiαaXa.e^{i\alpha_aX_a}\text{.}eiαa​Xa​.

Is eiαaXae^{i\alpha_aX_a}eiαa​Xa​ really an element of the group? You might worry, because 1+iαaXa1+i\alpha_aX_a1+iαa​Xa​ generally is not in the group for finite α;\alpha\text{;}α; it’s only the first-order approximation to a group element. But 1+iαaXa/n1+i\alpha_aX_a/n1+iαa​Xa​/n differs from a genuine group element (the one with parameters α/n\alpha/nα/n in the original labeling) only at order 1/n2.1/n^2\text{.}1/n2. Multiplying nnn such factors together builds up an error of order n⋅1n2=1n,n\cdot\tfrac{1}{n^2}=\tfrac1n\text{,}n⋅n21​=n1​, which goes to zero.11 This is a sketch, not a proof. A careful version has to check that the small errors aren’t amplified when they’re multiplied by the other factors, which is true because every factor is close to the identity. So eiαaXae^{i\alpha_aX_a}eiαa​Xa​ is the limit of products of genuine group elements (Fig. 1), and it’s in the group for every α,\alpha\text{,}α, not just to first order. The XaX_aXa​ are called the generators of the Lie group D(α).D(\alpha)\text{.}D(α).Figure 1

3Where structure constants come from

The generators of a non-commutative (“non-abelian”) Lie group don’t commute with each other, so in general

eiαaXaeiβbXb≠ei(αa+βa)Xa.e^{i\alpha_aX_a}e^{i\beta_bX_b} \neq e^{i(\alpha_a+\beta_a)X_a}.eiαa​Xa​eiβb​Xb​=ei(αa​+βa​)Xa​.
(3)

Nonetheless, the left side is a product of two group elements, so it’s a group element too. For small α\alphaα and β\betaβ it’s close to the identity, so it can be written as eiδaXae^{i\delta_aX_a}eiδa​Xa​ for some δ\deltaδ that depends on α\alphaα and β.\beta\text{.}β. The question is: what is δ?\delta\text{?}δ?

The strategy is to take the logarithm of both sides and expand in powers of the generators. This is the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff (BCH) approach: it turns a hard question about multiplying exponentials into an easier one about expanding a logarithm. To keep things short, write u≡αaXau\equiv\alpha_aX_au≡αa​Xa​ and v≡βbXb.v\equiv\beta_bX_b\text{.}v≡βb​Xb​. We want δ\deltaδ with

iδaXa=ln⁡ ⁣(eiueiv)=ln⁡(1+K),K≡eiueiv−1.i\delta_aX_a = \ln\!\big(e^{iu}e^{iv}\big) = \ln(1+K), \qquad K\equiv e^{iu}e^{iv}-1 .iδa​Xa​=ln(eiueiv)=ln(1+K),K≡eiueiv−1.
(4)

Expanding each exponential to second order and multiplying out,

K=(1+iu−12u2)(1+iv−12v2)−1+O(3)=iu+iv−uv−12u2−12v2+O(3).\begin{aligned} K &= \Big(1+iu-\tfrac12u^2\Big)\Big(1+iv-\tfrac12v^2\Big) - 1 + \order(3)\\ &= iu+iv-uv-\tfrac12u^2-\tfrac12v^2+\order(3). \end{aligned}K​=(1+iu−21​u2)(1+iv−21​v2)−1+O(3)=iu+iv−uv−21​u2−21​v2+O(3).​
(5)

Now use ln⁡(1+K)=K−12K2+O(K3).\ln(1+K)=K-\tfrac12K^2+\order(K^3)\text{.}ln(1+K)=K−21​K2+O(K3). Since KKK starts at first order, only its first-order part is needed in K2:K^2\text{:}K2:

K2=(iu+iv)2+O(3)=−u2−uv−vu−v2+O(3).K^2 = (iu+iv)^2 + \order(3) = -u^2-uv-vu-v^2 + \order(3).K2=(iu+iv)2+O(3)=−u2−uv−vu−v2+O(3).
(6)

Putting these together,

ln⁡(1+K)=[iu+iv−uv−12u2−12v2]−12[−u2−uv−vu−v2]+O(3)=iu+iv−uv+12uv+12vu+O(3)=iu+iv−12[u,v]+O(3).\begin{aligned} \ln(1+K) &= \Big[iu+iv-uv-\tfrac12u^2-\tfrac12v^2\Big]\\ &\qquad - \tfrac12\Big[-u^2-uv-vu-v^2\Big] + \order(3)\\ &= iu+iv - uv + \tfrac12uv+\tfrac12vu + \order(3)\\ &= iu+iv-\tfrac12[u,v] + \order(3). \end{aligned}ln(1+K)​=[iu+iv−uv−21​u2−21​v2]−21​[−u2−uv−vu−v2]+O(3)=iu+iv−uv+21​uv+21​vu+O(3)=iu+iv−21​[u,v]+O(3).​
(7)

Look at what happened. All the u2u^2u2 and v2v^2v2 terms cancelled, and the only thing left over from “squaring” the exponentials is the commutator [u,v][u,v][u,v] (Fig. 2). This is the second-order truncation of the full BCH formula, and it’s the reason that commutators are the central objects of Lie theory: to second order, the leftover from composing two group elements is entirely a commutator.Figure 2

When two exponentials collide,Their exponents can’t simply rideSide by side to the end:At second they bend,And a commutator’s all left inside.

So iδaXa=iu+iv−12[u,v]+O(3).i\delta_aX_a = iu+iv-\tfrac12[u,v]+\order(3)\text{.}iδa​Xa​=iu+iv−21​[u,v]+O(3). Rearranging,

[u,v]=[αaXa,βbXb]=−2i(δc−αc−βc)Xc+O(3).[u,v] = [\alpha_aX_a,\beta_bX_b] = -2i(\delta_c-\alpha_c-\beta_c)X_c + \order(3).[u,v]=[αa​Xa​,βb​Xb​]=−2i(δc​−αc​−βc​)Xc​+O(3).
(8)

The difference δc−αc−βc\delta_c-\alpha_c-\beta_cδc​−αc​−βc​ starts at second order in α\alphaα and β.\beta\text{.}β. Write its second-order part (the terms of degree two in α\alphaα and β\betaβ together) as −12γc.-\tfrac12\gamma_c\text{.}−21​γc​. The left side of eq. (8) is exactly second order, so matching the second-order terms on both sides gives

[αaXa,βbXb]=iγcXc,[\alpha_aX_a,\beta_bX_b] = i\gamma_cX_c ,[αa​Xa​,βb​Xb​]=iγc​Xc​,
(9)

exactly, as an identity between polynomials in α\alphaα and β.\beta\text{.}β.

Extracting the structure constants. The commutator is bilinear, linear in each argument separately, so the parameters come straight out of the bracket:

αaβb [Xa,Xb]=iγcXcfor all α,β.\alpha_a\beta_b\,[X_a,X_b] = i\gamma_cX_c\qquad\text{for all }\alpha,\beta.αa​βb​[Xa​,Xb​]=iγc​Xc​for all α,β.
(10)

Now let α\alphaα point along a single direction a,a\text{,}a, and β\betaβ along a single direction b:b\text{:}b: α=s e^a\alpha=s\,\hat e_aα=se^a​ and β=t e^b.\beta=t\,\hat e_b\text{.}β=te^b​. The left side becomes st [Xa,Xb],st\,[X_a,X_b]\text{,}st[Xa​,Xb​], and the right side is some linear combination of the Xc.X_c\text{.}Xc​. So [Xa,Xb][X_a,X_b][Xa​,Xb​] is itself a linear combination of the generators: the generators are closed under commutation. This isn’t an extra assumption; it’s a consequence of the group being closed under multiplication. The coefficients can depend only on a,a\text{,}a, bbb and c,c\text{,}c, since there’s no α\alphaα or β\betaβ anywhere in [Xa,Xb].[X_a,X_b]\text{.}[Xa​,Xb​]. Calling them ifabc,if_{abc}\text{,}ifabc​,

  [Xa,Xb]=ifabc Xc.  \boxed{\;[X_a,X_b] = if_{abc}\,X_c .\;}[Xa​,Xb​]=ifabc​Xc​.​
(11)

The numbers fabcf_{abc}fabc​ are the structure constants of the group.

You might wonder whether γc\gamma_cγc​ was secretly allowed to be more complicated. It’s a second-order polynomial in α\alphaα and β,\beta\text{,}β, so a priori it could contain αα\alpha\alphaαα and ββ\beta\betaββ terms as well as αβ\alpha\betaαβ ones. But the left side of eq. (10) is exactly bilinear, and the XcX_cXc​ are linearly independent, so each γc\gamma_cγc​ must be bilinear too: substituting eq. (11) back in gives γc=αaβbfabc,\gamma_c=\alpha_a\beta_bf_{abc}\text{,}γc​=αa​βb​fabc​, with coefficients that can’t depend on α\alphaα or β.\beta\text{.}β. Both the closure and the constants fabcf_{abc}fabc​ come out of the argument.

Two more facts follow quickly. Since [Xb,Xa]=−[Xa,Xb],[X_b,X_a]=-[X_a,X_b]\text{,}[Xb​,Xa​]=−[Xa​,Xb​], comparing coefficients of the linearly independent XcX_cXc​ gives

fbac=−fabc,f_{bac} = -f_{abc} ,fbac​=−fabc​,
(12)

so the structure constants are antisymmetric in their first two indices. And comparing coefficients of XcX_cXc​ in iδaXa=iu+iv−12[u,v]i\delta_aX_a=iu+iv-\tfrac12[u,v]iδa​Xa​=iu+iv−21​[u,v] gives δ\deltaδ explicitly:

δc=αc+βc−12αaβbfabc+⋯\delta_c = \alpha_c+\beta_c-\tfrac12\alpha_a\beta_bf_{abc}+\cdotsδc​=αc​+βc​−21​αa​βb​fabc​+⋯
(13)

4Why the structure constants are enough

Here’s a natural worry. Suppose we expanded ln⁡(eiueiv)\ln(e^{iu}e^{iv})ln(eiueiv) to third order instead of second. Might we find terms like X1X1X2,X_1X_1X_2\text{,}X1​X1​X2​, or X13,X_1^3\text{,}X13​, that can’t be built from any combination of commutators? To match the left side iδaXa,i\delta_aX_a\text{,}iδa​Xa​, which is linear in the generators, we’d then need extra rules such as Xa3=cbXb:X_a^3=c_bX_b\text{:}Xa3​=cb​Xb​: a whole new set of “third-order structure constants” on top of the fabc.f_{abc}\text{.}fabc​.

Fortunately this never happens. The Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff theorem guarantees that ln⁡(eiueiv),\ln(e^{iu}e^{iv})\text{,}ln(eiueiv), expanded to any order, is a sum of nested commutators of uuu and v,v\text{,}v, never a stand-alone term like X13.X_1^3\text{.}X13​. (Problem 1 checks this at third order.) Each nested commutator reduces, by repeated use of eq. (11), to a linear combination of the Xc,X_c\text{,}Xc​, with coefficients built from α,\alpha\text{,}α, β\betaβ and the fabc.f_{abc}\text{.}fabc​. So the commutation relations determine δa\delta_aδa​ completely, as an infinite series in α,\alpha\text{,}α, β\betaβ and fabcf_{abc}fabc​ alone. Going to higher order adds new terms to the series, but at every order the result is an exact linear combination of the Xa,X_a\text{,}Xa​, and no new constants are ever needed.

5Unitary representations have real structure constants

Symmetries in quantum mechanics are represented by unitary operators, so that probabilities are preserved. So it matters what unitarity implies for the generators. If every eiαaXae^{i\alpha_aX_a}eiαa​Xa​ is unitary, then differentiating (eiαaXa)†eiαaXa=1\big(e^{i\alpha_aX_a}\big)^\dagger e^{i\alpha_aX_a}=1(eiαa​Xa​)†eiαa​Xa​=1 with respect to αa\alpha_aαa​ at α=0\alpha=0α=0 gives −iXa†+iXa=0.-iX_a^\dagger+iX_a=0\text{.}−iXa†​+iXa​=0. So each XaX_aXa​ is Hermitian. Now take the Hermitian conjugate of the structure-constant relation:

[Xa,Xb]†=(ifabcXc)†=−ifabc∗Xc.[X_a,X_b]^\dagger = \big(if_{abc}X_c\big)^\dagger = -if_{abc}^*X_c.[Xa​,Xb​]†=(ifabc​Xc​)†=−ifabc∗​Xc​.
(14)

But using (XaXb)†=Xb†Xa†=XbXa,(X_aX_b)^\dagger=X_b^\dagger X_a^\dagger=X_bX_a\text{,}(Xa​Xb​)†=Xb†​Xa†​=Xb​Xa​, we also have

[Xa,Xb]†=XbXa−XaXb=−[Xa,Xb]=−ifabcXc.[X_a,X_b]^\dagger = X_bX_a-X_aX_b = -[X_a,X_b] = -if_{abc}X_c.[Xa​,Xb​]†=Xb​Xa​−Xa​Xb​=−[Xa​,Xb​]=−ifabc​Xc​.
(15)

Comparing coefficients of the linearly independent XcX_cXc​ gives fabc∗=fabc:f_{abc}^*=f_{abc}\text{:}fabc∗​=fabc​: the structure constants of a unitary representation are real.

6The Jacobi identity and the adjoint representation

Any commutator built from an associative product satisfies the Jacobi identity,

[Xa,[Xb,Xc]]+[Xb,[Xc,Xa]]+[Xc,[Xa,Xb]]=0.[X_a,[X_b,X_c]] + [X_b,[X_c,X_a]] + [X_c,[X_a,X_b]] = 0.[Xa​,[Xb​,Xc​]]+[Xb​,[Xc​,Xa​]]+[Xc​,[Xa​,Xb​]]=0.
(16)

This is an algebraic identity, not a new assumption (Exercise 4). Expanding the first term with the structure constants twice,

[Xa,[Xb,Xc]]=[Xa,ifbcdXd]=ifbcd[Xa,Xd]=ifbcd⋅ifadeXe=−fbcdfadeXe,\begin{aligned} [X_a,[X_b,X_c]] &= [X_a,if_{bcd}X_d] = if_{bcd}[X_a,X_d]\\ &= if_{bcd}\cdot if_{ade}X_e = -f_{bcd}f_{ade}X_e, \end{aligned}[Xa​,[Xb​,Xc​]]​=[Xa​,ifbcd​Xd​]=ifbcd​[Xa​,Xd​]=ifbcd​⋅ifade​Xe​=−fbcd​fade​Xe​,​
(17)

and cyclically permuting (a,b,c)(a,b,c)(a,b,c) for the other two terms, the Jacobi identity turns into a purely numerical identity among the structure constants (by linear independence of the Xe).X_e\text{).}Xe​). It has free indices a,b,c,e:a,b,c,e\text{:}a,b,c,e:

fbcdfade+fcadfbde+fabdfcde=0.f_{bcd}f_{ade} + f_{cad}f_{bde} + f_{abd}f_{cde} = 0.fbcd​fade​+fcad​fbde​+fabd​fcde​=0.
(18)

The adjoint representation. Define N×NN\times NN×N matrices TaT_aTa​ by reading the structure constants off as matrix entries:

[Ta]bc≡−ifabc.[T_a]_{bc}\equiv-if_{abc}.[Ta​]bc​≡−ifabc​.
(19)

Then

[Ta,Tb]pq=[Ta]pd[Tb]dq−[Tb]pd[Ta]dq=−fapdfbdq+fbpdfadq.[T_a,T_b]_{pq} = [T_a]_{pd}[T_b]_{dq} - [T_b]_{pd}[T_a]_{dq} = -f_{apd}f_{bdq} + f_{bpd}f_{adq}.[Ta​,Tb​]pq​=[Ta​]pd​[Tb​]dq​−[Tb​]pd​[Ta​]dq​=−fapd​fbdq​+fbpd​fadq​.
(20)

The Jacobi identity (18) with c→pc\to pc→p and e→qe\to qe→q reads fbpdfadq+fpadfbdq+fabdfpdq=0.f_{bpd}f_{adq} + f_{pad}f_{bdq} + f_{abd}f_{pdq} = 0\text{.}fbpd​fadq​+fpad​fbdq​+fabd​fpdq​=0. Using the antisymmetry (12), fpad=−fapdf_{pad}=-f_{apd}fpad​=−fapd​ and fpdq=−fdpq,f_{pdq}=-f_{dpq}\text{,}fpdq​=−fdpq​, so

−fapdfbdq+fbpdfadq=fabdfdpq=ifabd (−ifdpq)=ifabd [Td]pq.\begin{aligned} -f_{apd}f_{bdq} + f_{bpd}f_{adq} &= f_{abd}f_{dpq} = if_{abd}\,\big(-if_{dpq}\big)\\ &= if_{abd}\,[T_d]_{pq}. \end{aligned}−fapd​fbdq​+fbpd​fadq​​=fabd​fdpq​=ifabd​(−ifdpq​)=ifabd​[Td​]pq​.​
(21)

Hence

[Ta,Tb]=ifabc Tc.[T_a,T_b] = if_{abc}\,T_c .[Ta​,Tb​]=ifabc​Tc​.

The matrices TaT_aTa​ obey the same commutation relations as the generators, so they generate a representation of the group, built from the structure constants alone. It acts on an NNN-dimensional space, with one dimension per generator, and it’s called the adjoint representation. Up to a transpose and a sign, which both disappear once fabcf_{abc}fabc​ is totally antisymmetric (Section 9), TaT_aTa​ is the matrix of the map X↦[Xa,X]:X\mapsto[X_a,X]\text{:}X↦[Xa​,X]: each generator is represented by what it does, through the bracket, to all the generators.

7A scalar product on the generators

From here on, TaT_aTa​ denotes the matrix of XaX_aXa​ in the adjoint representation. On the space of these matrices, define the scalar product

⟨Ta,Tb⟩≡Tr⁡[TaTb]≡Mab.\langle T_a,T_b\rangle \equiv \Tr[T_aT_b] \equiv M_{ab}.⟨Ta​,Tb​⟩≡Tr[Ta​Tb​]≡Mab​.
(23)

This is the Killing form, evaluated on the Hermitian generators.22 Mathematicians usually evaluate it on the anti-Hermitian combinations iXa,iX_a\text{,}iXa​, which flips its sign. That’s why “compact” goes with positive values here and with negative ones in mathematics books. The indices run from 1 to N,N\text{,}N, so the scalar products form an N×NN\times NN×N matrix M.M\text{.}M. It’s

  • symmetric, because Tr⁡[TaTb]=Tr⁡[TbTa]\Tr[T_aT_b]=\Tr[T_bT_a]Tr[Ta​Tb​]=Tr[Tb​Ta​] (the trace is cyclic); and
  • real, because for a unitary representation the fabcf_{abc}fabc​ are real. That makes each TaT_aTa​ purely imaginary, and a product of two purely imaginary matrices is real.
  1. Mathematicians usually evaluate it on the anti-Hermitian combinations iXa,iX_a\text{,}iXa​, which flips its sign. That’s why “compact” goes with positive values here and with negative ones in mathematics books. ↩

The generators are only defined up to a change of basis. Take a real, invertible N×NN\times NN×N matrix LLL and new generators

Xa→Xa′=LabXb.X_a\to X_a'=L_{ab}X_b.Xa​→Xa′​=Lab​Xb​.
(24)

[Xa′,Xb′]=LadLbe[Xd,Xe]=iLadLbefdegXg=iLadLbefdeg(L−1)gcXc′.\begin{aligned} [X_a',X_b'] &= L_{ad}L_{be}[X_d,X_e] = iL_{ad}L_{be}f_{deg}X_g\\ &= iL_{ad}L_{be}f_{deg}\big(L^{-1}\big)_{gc}X_c'. \end{aligned}[Xa′​,Xb′​]​=Lad​Lbe​[Xd​,Xe​]=iLad​Lbe​fdeg​Xg​=iLad​Lbe​fdeg​(L−1)gc​Xc′​.​
(25)

So the structure constants transform as

fabc→fabc′=LadLbefdeg(L−1)gc.f_{abc}\to f'_{abc} = L_{ad}L_{be}f_{deg}\big(L^{-1}\big)_{gc}.fabc​→fabc′​=Lad​Lbe​fdeg​(L−1)gc​.
(26)

The new structure constants give a new adjoint representation:

[Ta′]bc=−ifabc′=Lad Lbe [Td]eg (L−1)gc=Lad [LTdL−1]bc,\begin{aligned} [T_a']_{bc} = -if'_{abc} &= L_{ad}\,L_{be}\,[T_d]_{eg}\,\big(L^{-1}\big)_{gc}\\ &= L_{ad}\,\big[LT_dL^{-1}\big]_{bc}, \end{aligned}[Ta′​]bc​=−ifabc′​​=Lad​Lbe​[Td​]eg​(L−1)gc​=Lad​[LTd​L−1]bc​,​

that is,

Ta′=Lad (LTdL−1).T_a' = L_{ad}\,\big(LT_dL^{-1}\big).Ta′​=Lad​(LTd​L−1).
(28)

So a linear change of the generators does two things to the adjoint representation: it recombines the matrices in the same way, Td→LadTd,T_d\to L_{ad}T_d\text{,}Td​→Lad​Td​, and it applies a similarity transformation T→LTL−1T\to LTL^{-1}T→LTL−1 to each one. Do these two operations commute? Yes, because conjugation is linear and the LadL_{ad}Lad​ are just numbers: L(∑dLadTd)L−1=∑dLad(LTdL−1).L\big(\sum_d L_{ad}T_d\big)L^{-1} = \sum_d L_{ad}\big(LT_dL^{-1}\big)\text{.}L(∑d​Lad​Td​)L−1=∑d​Lad​(LTd​L−1).

The effect on the scalar product follows from the cyclic property of the trace:

(29)

(The matrices TcT_cTc​ and TdT_dTd​ can’t be rearranged inside the trace, but the numbers LacL_{ac}Lac​ and LbdL_{bd}Lbd​ can be moved anywhere.) In matrix language,

M→M′=LMLT.M\to M' = LML^T.M→M′=LMLT.

9Compact Lie algebras

MMM is real and symmetric, so it can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix, M=QΛQT.M=Q\Lambda Q^T\text{.}M=QΛQT. Choosing L=QTL=Q^TL=QT in eq. (30) gives

M′=QT(QΛQT)Q=Λ,Λ=diag⁡(k1,…,kN),M' = Q^T\big(Q\Lambda Q^T\big)Q = \Lambda,\qquad \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(k^1,\dots,k^N),M′=QT(QΛQT)Q=Λ,Λ=diag(k1,…,kN),
(31)

that is, Tr⁡[Ta′Tb′]=kaδab,\Tr[T_a'T_b'] = k^a\delta_{ab}\text{,}Tr[Ta′​Tb′​]=kaδab​, with no sum over a.a\text{.}a. A further diagonal L=diag⁡(μ1,…,μN)L=\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_N)L=diag(μ1​,…,μN​) rescales ka→μa2 ka.k^a\to\mu_a^2\,k^a\text{.}ka→μa2​ka. So by varying LLL we can change the size of each ka,k^a\text{,}ka, but not its sign, since LLL appears twice in M→LMLT.M\to LML^T\text{.}M→LMLT. More generally, by Sylvester’s law of inertia, no real change of basis can change the numbers of positive, negative and zero kak^aka’s. So the following definition doesn’t depend on the basis.

A Lie algebra is called compact if every kak^aka is positive.33 The name comes from the group: for these algebras the group manifold is compact, like the three-sphere that is SU(2).SU(2)\text{.}SU(2). We won’t prove the connection here. In that case we can rescale every kak^aka to one common constant λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 by a suitable choice of L,L\text{,}L, which gives

Tr⁡[TaTb]=λ δab.\Tr[T_aT_b]=\lambda\,\delta_{ab}.Tr[Ta​Tb​]=λδab​.
(32)

From here on we work in such a basis, and drop the primes. In this basis the structure constants can be read off from a trace:

Tr⁡[[Ta,Tb]Tc]=ifabdTr⁡[TdTc]=ifabd λ δdc=iλfabc,\Tr\big[[T_a,T_b]T_c\big] = if_{abd}\Tr[T_dT_c] = if_{abd}\,\lambda\,\delta_{dc} = i\lambda f_{abc},Tr[[Ta​,Tb​]Tc​]=ifabd​Tr[Td​Tc​]=ifabd​λδdc​=iλfabc​,
(33)

so

fabc=−iλTr⁡[[Ta,Tb]Tc].f_{abc} = -\frac{i}{\lambda}\Tr\big[[T_a,T_b]T_c\big].fabc​=−λi​Tr[[Ta​,Tb​]Tc​].
(34)

The structure constants are completely antisymmetric. By the cyclic property of the trace,

Tr⁡[[Ta,Tb]Tc]=Tr⁡[TaTbTc−TbTaTc]=Tr⁡[TbTcTa−TcTbTa]=Tr⁡[[Tb,Tc]Ta],\begin{aligned} \Tr\big[[T_a,T_b]T_c\big] &= \Tr[T_aT_bT_c - T_bT_aT_c]\\ &= \Tr[T_bT_cT_a - T_cT_bT_a] = \Tr\big[[T_b,T_c]T_a\big], \end{aligned}Tr[[Ta​,Tb​]Tc​]​=Tr[Ta​Tb​Tc​−Tb​Ta​Tc​]=Tr[Tb​Tc​Ta​−Tc​Tb​Ta​]=Tr[[Tb​,Tc​]Ta​],​
(35)

so fabc=fbca.f_{abc}=f_{bca}\text{.}fabc​=fbca​. Combined with the antisymmetry fabc=−fbacf_{abc}=-f_{bac}fabc​=−fbac​ we already had,

fabc=fbca=fcab,fabc=−fbac=−fcba=−facb:f_{abc}=f_{bca}=f_{cab}, \qquad f_{abc}=-f_{bac}=-f_{cba}=-f_{acb}:fabc​=fbca​=fcab​,fabc​=−fbac​=−fcba​=−facb​:
(36)

cyclic permutations change nothing, and swapping any two indices flips the sign. This holds in the basis where Tr⁡[TaTb]=λδab,\Tr[T_aT_b]=\lambda\delta_{ab}\text{,}Tr[Ta​Tb​]=λδab​, and a generic change of basis destroys it. Orthogonal changes of basis (LLT=1)\text{(}LL^T=1\text{)}(LLT=1) preserve Tr⁡[TaTb]=λδab,\Tr[T_aT_b]=\lambda\delta_{ab}\text{,}Tr[Ta​Tb​]=λδab​, and hence total antisymmetry. In this basis each TaT_aTa​ is purely imaginary and antisymmetric, hence Hermitian, and TaT_aTa​ is exactly the matrix of the map X↦[Xa,X].X\mapsto[X_a,X]\text{.}X↦[Xa​,X].

10Invariant subalgebras and simple algebras

A subset of the generators spans an invariant subalgebra if bracketing any of its elements with any generator of the whole algebra lands back inside it: if XXX is in the invariant subalgebra and YYY is any generator, then [X,Y][X,Y][X,Y] is again in the invariant subalgebra. By linearity, the same then holds for any combination YYY of generators.

Exponentiating an invariant subalgebra gives an invariant subgroup. Let XXX be in the invariant subalgebra, and let YYY be any element of the algebra. Conjugation by an invertible matrix commutes with taking powers, S−1XnS=(S−1XS)n,S^{-1}X^nS=(S^{-1}XS)^n\text{,}S−1XnS=(S−1XS)n, and hence with exponentiation, so

(eiY)−1eiXeiY=eiX′,X′≡e−iYXeiY.\big(e^{iY}\big)^{-1}e^{iX}e^{iY} = e^{iX'},\qquad X'\equiv e^{-iY}Xe^{iY}.(eiY)−1eiXeiY=eiX′,X′≡e−iYXeiY.
(37)

Expanding, and keeping everything up to second order in Y,Y\text{,}Y,

e−iYXeiY=(1−iY−12Y2) X (1+iY−12Y2)=X−iYX+iXY−12Y2X+YXY−12XY2=X−i(YX−XY)−12(Y2X−2YXY+XY2)=X−i[Y,X]−12[Y,[Y,X]]+O(Y3).\begin{aligned} e^{-iY}Xe^{iY} &= \Big(1-iY-\tfrac12Y^2\Big)\,X\,\Big(1+iY-\tfrac12Y^2\Big)\\ &= X - iYX + iXY - \tfrac12Y^2X + YXY - \tfrac12XY^2\\ &= X - i(YX-XY) - \tfrac12\big(Y^2X-2YXY+XY^2\big)\\ &= X - i[Y,X] - \tfrac12[Y,[Y,X]] + \order(Y^3). \end{aligned}e−iYXeiY​=(1−iY−21​Y2)X(1+iY−21​Y2)=X−iYX+iXY−21​Y2X+YXY−21​XY2=X−i(YX−XY)−21​(Y2X−2YXY+XY2)=X−i[Y,X]−21​[Y,[Y,X]]+O(Y3).​
(38)

At every order the correction is a nested commutator [Y,[Y,…[Y,X]]],[Y,[Y,\dots[Y,X]]]\text{,}[Y,[Y,…[Y,X]]], and each one lands back in the invariant subalgebra, by definition. So X′X'X′ is in the invariant subalgebra too, and eiX′e^{iX'}eiX′ is in the corresponding subgroup: conjugation by any group element eiYe^{iY}eiY can’t push you out of it. The subgroup is invariant.

Every Lie algebra has two trivial invariant subalgebras: {0},\{0\}\text{,}{0}, and the whole algebra. A Lie algebra is simple if it has no others.44 A single generator, as for U(1),U(1)\text{,}U(1), trivially qualifies, but it’s conventionally excluded: “simple” is reserved for non-abelian algebras.

Remark: Don’t confuse simple with irreducible. Simplicity is a property of the generators and their commutators, an algebraic statement. Irreducibility is a property of a representation: whether the vector space it acts on contains a smaller invariant subspace. The theorem in the next section connects the two for one particular representation, the adjoint. ♣\clubsuit♣

  1. A single generator, as for U(1),U(1)\text{,}U(1), trivially qualifies, but it’s conventionally excluded: “simple” is reserved for non-abelian algebras. ↩

11Simple and compact means an irreducible adjoint

Theorem 1 (Simple and compact). If a Lie algebra is simple, and compact, so that Tr⁡[TaTb]=λδab\Tr[T_aT_b]=\lambda\delta_{ab}Tr[Ta​Tb​]=λδab​ in a suitable basis, then its adjoint representation is irreducible.

First the setting. The adjoint representation acts on NNN-component vectors ξ,\xi\text{,}ξ, one component per generator. Work in the compact basis, where fabcf_{abc}fabc​ is totally antisymmetric. There [Ta]cb=−ifacb=ifabc,[T_a]_{cb}=-if_{acb}=if_{abc}\text{,}[Ta​]cb​=−ifacb​=ifabc​, so TaξT_a\xiTa​ξ lists the coefficients of [Xa,ξbXb]=ifabcξbXc:[X_a,\xi_bX_b]=if_{abc}\xi_bX_c\text{:}[Xa​,ξb​Xb​]=ifabc​ξb​Xc​: TaT_aTa​ is the matrix of X↦[Xa,X].X\mapsto[X_a,X]\text{.}X↦[Xa​,X]. Reducibility would mean a subspace W,W\text{,}W, with 0<dim⁡W<N,0<\dim W<N\text{,}0<dimW<N, that every TaT_aTa​ maps into itself. We take WWW to be spanned by real vectors ξ,\xi\text{,}ξ, that is, by real combinations of generators; complex subspaces come after the proof.

Proof. Suppose the adjoint representation were reducible, with an invariant subspace WWW of dimension m,m\text{,}m, where 0<m<N.0<m<N\text{.}0<m<N. Choose a real orthonormal basis of the space of generators whose first mmm vectors span W.W\text{.}W. This is an orthogonal change of basis, so Tr⁡[TaTb]=λδab\Tr[T_aT_b]=\lambda\delta_{ab}Tr[Ta​Tb​]=λδab​ and total antisymmetry survive it. In the new basis, WWW is spanned by X1,…,Xm.X_1,\dots,X_m\text{.}X1​,…,Xm​. Let rrr label the first group, r∈{1,…,m},r\in\{1,\dots,m\}\text{,}r∈{1,…,m}, and xxx the second, x∈{m+1,…,N}.x\in\{m+1,\dots,N\}\text{.}x∈{m+1,…,N}. Invariance of WWW says that TaT_aTa​ never maps an rrr-direction into an xxx-direction:

[Ta]xr=−ifaxr=0for every a, x, r.[T_a]_{xr} = -if_{axr} = 0\qquad\text{for every } a,\ x,\ r.[Ta​]xr​=−ifaxr​=0for every a, x, r.
(39)

The index aaa is itself either one of the xxx’s or one of the rrr’s, so both fx1x2r=0f_{x_1x_2r}=0fx1​x2​r​=0 and fr1xr2=0.f_{r_1xr_2}=0\text{.}fr1​xr2​​=0. By total antisymmetry, every structure constant that carries indices from both groups is a permutation of one of these, so it vanishes too. The only nonzero fabcf_{abc}fabc​’s are of the form fr1r2r3f_{r_1r_2r_3}fr1​r2​r3​​ or fx1x2x3,f_{x_1x_2x_3}\text{,}fx1​x2​x3​​, and every TaT_aTa​ is block-diagonal (Fig. 3).Figure 3 So the whole algebra breaks into two pieces. Bracketing any XrX_rXr​ with any XxX_xXx​ gives zero, and bracketing it with another XrX_rXr​ stays inside the first group. So {X1,…,Xm}\{X_1,\dots,X_m\}{X1​,…,Xm​} is a non-trivial invariant subalgebra, and so is {Xm+1,…,XN}.\{X_{m+1},\dots,X_N\}\text{.}{Xm+1​,…,XN​}. This contradicts simplicity, which allows no non-trivial invariant subalgebras. So the adjoint representation can’t be reducible.□\square□

Remarks: 1. Here’s the idea in one sentence. Reducibility of the adjoint representation would mean that the generators split into two blocks that never interact through the bracket, and two non-interacting blocks are each, by definition, an invariant subalgebra, which simplicity forbids. Compactness enters through total antisymmetry. It converts the invariance of W,W\text{,}W, faxr=0,f_{axr}=0\text{,}faxr​=0, which is a statement about the matrices Ta,T_a\text{,}Ta​, into frax=0,f_{rax}=0\text{,}frax​=0, which is a statement about the brackets [Xr,Xa].[X_r,X_a]\text{.}[Xr​,Xa​]. And it makes the other off-diagonal block vanish as well.

2. The proof uses a real orthogonal change of basis, so it shows that no invariant subspace is spanned by real combinations of generators. The theorem also holds for complex invariant subspaces, which is what matters in quantum mechanics, but that needs one more fact: for a compact simple algebra, allowing complex combinations of generators creates no new invariant subalgebras. Here compactness is essential. The Lorentz algebra is simple as a real algebra, but over the complex numbers its adjoint representation splits in two: the self-dual and anti-self-dual parts of an antisymmetric tensor Fμν.F_{\mu\nu}\text{.}Fμν​. ♣\clubsuit♣

12U(1)U(1)U(1) factors

A U(1)U(1)U(1) factor of a group is an invariant subalgebra containing a single generator, which commutes with every other generator of the group. If XaX_aXa​ is a U(1)U(1)U(1) generator, then [Xa,Xb]=ifabcXc=0[X_a,X_b]=if_{abc}X_c=0[Xa​,Xb​]=ifabc​Xc​=0 for every b,b\text{,}b, so fabc=0f_{abc}=0fabc​=0 for every bbb and c.c\text{.}c. Since [Ta]bc=−ifabc,[T_a]_{bc}=-if_{abc}\text{,}[Ta​]bc​=−ifabc​, this means that TaT_aTa​ is the zero matrix: in the adjoint representation, a U(1)U(1)U(1) generator is represented by nothing at all. That has two consequences.

The scalar product can’t see it. Row aaa of Mab=Tr⁡[TaTb]M_{ab}=\Tr[T_aT_b]Mab​=Tr[Ta​Tb​] vanishes, so MMM has a zero eigenvalue, and by Sylvester’s law some ka=0k^a=0ka=0 in every diagonal basis. So an algebra with a U(1)U(1)U(1) factor is never compact in the strict sense defined above (every ka>0).k^a>0\text{).}ka>0). That definition really describes compact algebras without U(1)U(1)U(1) factors, the compact semisimple ones. For example, SU(2)×U(1),SU(2)\times U(1)\text{,}SU(2)×U(1), with generators 12σ1,2,3\tfrac12\sigma_{1,2,3}21​σ1,2,3​ and 121,\tfrac12\mathbb 1\text{,}21​1, gives Tr⁡[TaTb]=diag⁡(2,2,2,0).\Tr[T_aT_b]=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,2,0)\text{.}Tr[Ta​Tb​]=diag(2,2,2,0).

It’s missing from every slot. Where fabcf_{abc}fabc​ is totally antisymmetric, the vanishing of fabcf_{abc}fabc​ with the U(1)U(1)U(1) index in the first slot implies that it vanishes in every slot,

fabc=fcab=fbca=−fbac=−fcba=−facb=0,f_{abc}=f_{cab}=f_{bca}=-f_{bac}=-f_{cba}=-f_{acb}=0,fabc​=fcab​=fbca​=−fbac​=−fcba​=−facb​=0,
(40)

so XaX_aXa​ also never appears on the right side of any commutator. Compact groups with U(1)U(1)U(1) factors, such as U(2),U(2)\text{,}U(2), do have bases with totally antisymmetric fabcf_{abc}fabc​ (the basis above is one), but that comes from a positive-definite invariant scalar product other than Tr⁡[TaTb],\Tr[T_aT_b]\text{,}Tr[Ta​Tb​], which vanishes in the U(1)U(1)U(1) direction (Exercise 5).

Remark: A U(1)U(1)U(1) generator contributes only zeros to the array of structure constants, in a totally antisymmetric basis, which is exactly what an absent direction would contribute. So the list of nonzero fabcf_{abc}fabc​’s can never tell you how many U(1)U(1)U(1) factors a Lie algebra has, and the scalar product Tr⁡[TaTb]\Tr[T_aT_b]Tr[Ta​Tb​] built from them is equally blind. That’s why, in classifying compact Lie algebras, the non-abelian (“semisimple”) part is fixed by its structure constants, while the number of U(1)U(1)U(1) factors has to be supplied separately. ♣\clubsuit♣

Two of the kak^aka’s are negative, and by Sylvester’s law no change of basis can fix that, so the algebra is not compact. Nor are its structure constants totally antisymmetric: f312=1,f_{312}=1\text{,}f312​=1, but the cyclically related f123=−1.f_{123}=-1\text{.}f123​=−1.

Remark: The signs match the geometry. JJJ generates rotations, whose parameter is an angle that comes back to itself, while the KKK’s generate boosts, whose rapidities run off to infinity. The 3×33\times33×3 matrices that realize these commutators on spacetime vectors make the point: the ones for K1K_1K1​ and K2K_2K2​ are anti-Hermitian, so eiαKe^{i\alpha K}eiαK is a boost, not a unitary matrix. In fact a non-compact simple group like this one has no finite-dimensional unitary representations except the trivial one. ♣\clubsuit♣
